canonical:
A stone. Still a stone. Surely something will happen soon—no, it’s a stone. Nothing happens on the screen. That goes on for five minutes. But you, the viewer, can still get one thing done: cut someone else’s reward.

This sounds grim all of a sudden, but it’s about an online experiment with participants in the United States. They were randomly assigned to watch either a five-minute video of a stone, where nothing happened, or a video of a magician.

During that time, they had three choices: reduce another participant’s reward, increase it, or do nothing. They could change it by 10 cents at a time, up to a maximum of 50 cents. The stone on the screen stayed silent, while the viewers were handed “a little power.”

So, did boredom become fuel for meanness?

canonical:
It is like someone saying, “I won’t drive,” while helping put fuel in a car. Not taking the wheel is different from not supporting the journey. But this comparison cannot settle who is responsible for military support. What we need to check is what the words cover.

So if you sum it up as “Britain won’t attack,” you stretch what was said about the Typhoon mission too far, making it cover all support. On the other hand, looking at what the refueling support covers and saying, “Then the Typhoons will attack too,” goes beyond the evidence.

The tools you need to read news are not a magnifying glass, but three questions: “Who?” “For which mission?” “Doing what?” Don’t leave after seeing only the big sign that says “to protect”; check the name tag underneath it too. Just putting one subject back can change how the news looks.

The most important question in the new space-security story is not simply whether satellites can be attacked.

It is this:

Is the weapon itself in orbit?

On September 14, 2026, U.S. Air Force Secretary Troy Meink said that the United States was deploying space-control weapons in orbit. He said they were meant to protect U.S. forces from hostile actions.

An official U.S. Space Force article published the next day described this as the first public acknowledgment that the Space Force had put weapons in orbit.

canonical:
The same pattern appeared in 2026. Small pouches appeared at Prada, Loewe, Miu Miu, and Valentino. At the same time, very large bags appeared at Celine, Altuzarra, Toteme, Stella McCartney, and Kallmeyer. Some Fall/Winter 2026 shoulder bags from Chanel, Miu Miu, and Bottega Veneta were even large enough for a laptop.

Mini bags also received strong attention from fashion editors. One fashion magazine called them a major Fall 2026 styling direction. But another offered a more mixed view, saying that autumn was bringing back larger bags while still keeping smaller clutches and top-handle bags in the picture.

One trend company also reported a 152% rise in retail adoption for oversized clutches in 2026. That is a company estimate, but it adds an important counterpoint.

The clearest answer is this: tiny bags are gaining attention in some fashion spaces, but they are not winning everywhere. Small and large bags are appearing side by side.
